claim: Carboxysomes are protein-based bacterial organelles encapsulating key enzymes of the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle.
source: Carboxysomes are protein-based bacterial organelles encapsulating key enzymes of the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about carboxysomes presented in the abstract, supported by established scientific knowledge about these structures.

claim: A ParA-like protein (McdA) is important for spatially organizing carboxysomes along the longitudinal axis of Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942.
source: Previous work has implicated a ParA-like protein (hereafter McdA) as important for spatially organizing carboxysomes along the longitudinal axis of the model cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942.
evidence: This claim references previous work, indicating it is supported by prior research citations.

claim: McdB localizes to carboxysomes.
source: Here, we identify a small protein, termed McdB that localizes to carboxysomes and drives emergent oscillatory patterning of McdA on the nucleoid.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: McdB drives emergent oscillatory patterning of McdA on the nucleoid.
source: Here, we identify a small protein, termed McdB that localizes to carboxysomes and drives emergent oscillatory patterning of McdA on the nucleoid.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental observations in the study.

claim: McdB directly stimulates McdA ATPase activity.
source: Our results demonstrate that McdB directly stimulates McdA ATPase activity and its release from DNA, driving carboxysome-dependent depletion of McdA locally on the nucleoid and promoting directed motion of carboxysomes towards increased concentrations of McdA.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro biochemical assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: McdB stimulates McdA release from DNA.
source: Our results demonstrate that McdB directly stimulates McdA ATPase activity and its release from DNA, driving carboxysome-dependent depletion of McdA locally on the nucleoid and promoting directed motion of carboxysomes towards increased concentrations of McdA.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA and other biochemical data in the manuscript.

claim: McdB drives carboxysome-dependent depletion of McdA locally on the nucleoid.
source: Our results demonstrate that McdB directly stimulates McdA ATPase activity and its release from DNA, driving carboxysome-dependent depletion of McdA locally on the nucleoid and promoting directed motion of carboxysomes towards increased concentrations of McdA.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing McdA depletion zones around carboxysomes.

claim: Carboxysomes move towards increased concentrations of McdA.
source: Our results demonstrate that McdB directly stimulates McdA ATPase activity and its release from DNA, driving carboxysome-dependent depletion of McdA locally on the nucleoid and promoting directed motion of carboxysomes towards increased concentrations of McdA.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data showing carboxysome movement.

claim: McdA and McdB utilize a Brownian-ratchet mechanism to position carboxysomes in cyanobacteria.
source: We propose that McdA and McdB are a previously unknown class of self-organizing proteins that utilize a Brownian-ratchet mechanism to position carboxysomes in cyanobacteria, rather than a cytoskeletal system.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental data and computational simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: McdA and McdB do not utilize a cytoskeletal system for carboxysome positioning.
source: We propose that McdA and McdB are a previously unknown class of self-organizing proteins that utilize a Brownian-ratchet mechanism to position carboxysomes in cyanobacteria, rather than a cytoskeletal system.
evidence: This is supported by the absence of filament formation in vitro and the proposed alternative mechanism.

claim: Over 23 different classes of bacterial microcompartments are broadly distributed across bacterial phyla.
source: Over 23 different classes of BMC are broadly distributed across bacterial phyla, but perhaps the best characterized class are the large (~175 nm) carbon-fixing carboxysomes of cyanobacteria (reviewed here: Rae et al., 2013; Kerfeld and Melnicki, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Carboxysomes are approximately 175 nm in size.
source: Over 23 different classes of BMC are broadly distributed across bacterial phyla, but perhaps the best characterized class are the large (~175 nm) carbon-fixing carboxysomes of cyanobacteria (reviewed here: Rae et al., 2013; Kerfeld and Melnicki, 2016).
evidence: This is a measurement cited from the literature.

claim: Carboxysomes encapsulate RuBisCO and carbonic anhydrase.
source: Carboxysomes encapsulate the key Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle enzyme, ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RuBisCO), and enhance the carbon fixation efficiency of this enzyme by creating a microenvironment that is enriched for CO2. Specifically, carboxysomes consist of an outer 'shell' layer that encapsulates both RuBisCO and carbonic anhydrase
evidence: This is established knowledge about carboxysome composition.

claim: Localized conversion of bicarbonate to CO2 near RuBisCO reduces its oxygenase activity.
source: the localized conversion of bicarbonate to CO2 near RuBisCO is thought to greatly reduce its oxygenase activity, thereby suppressing the energetically-costly process of photorespiration (Rae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by citation.

claim: Carboxysomes align along the longitudinal axis of Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942.
source: In the model rod-shaped cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942 (hereafter S. elongatus), it has been shown that carboxysomes align along the longitudinal axis of the cell (Savage et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Equidistant positioning of carboxysomes promotes equal inheritance to both daughter cells.
source: This equidistant positioning is thought to promote equal inheritance of carboxysomes to both daughters of a dividing cell, which has been shown to impact cyanobacterial fitness under ambient CO2 (Savage et al., 2010; Rae et al., 2013; Kerfeld and Melnicki, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cyanobacteria contribute to greater than 25% of global carbon-fixation.
source: Since cyanobacteria contribute to greater than 25% of global carbon-fixation, how carboxysome organization is maintained is of considerable ecological importance.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cyanobacterial contribution to global carbon cycling.

claim: McdA displayed oscillatory dynamics in S. elongatus.
source: The most comprehensive study of BMC positioning to date showed that a ParA-type ATPase (hereafter McdA - Maintenance of carboxysome distribution A) displayed oscillatory dynamics in S. elongatus and was required for proper positioning of carboxysomes (Savage et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: McdA is required for proper positioning of carboxysomes.
source: The most comprehensive study of BMC positioning to date showed that a ParA-type ATPase (hereafter McdA - Maintenance of carboxysome distribution A) displayed oscillatory dynamics in S. elongatus and was required for proper positioning of carboxysomes (Savage et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ParA family members are important for segregation of bacterial chromosomes and low-copy plasmids.
source: ParA family members have been most comprehensively studied as factors important for the segregation of genetic material; bacterial chromosomes and low-copy plasmids (reviewed here: Baxter and Funnell, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Early hypotheses favored a cytoskeletal model for ParA function.
source: Early hypotheses of ParA function favored a cytoskeletal model in which ParA formed filaments that self-assemble into a larger scaffold capable of segregating genetic cargo, analogous to a primitive mitotic spindle (Ringgaard et al., 2009; Ptacin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In vitro observations showed fibrous, long bundled filaments of purified ParA/MinD family proteins.
source: These models were supported in part by in vitro observations of fibrous, long bundled filaments of purified members of the ParA/MinD family of proteins (Reviewed here: Vecchiarelli et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: Filament-based models of ParA have been challenged by recent experiments.
source: More recently, filament-based models of ParA have been challenged by experiments utilizing reconstituted cell-free systems (Hwang et al., 2013; Vecchiarelli et al., 2013; Vecchiarelli et al., 2014), super-resolution microscopy (Le Gall et al., 2016; Lim et al., 2014), crystallography (Zhang and Schumacher, 2017), and mathematical modelling approaches (Hu et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2017; Le Gall et al., 2016; Lim et al., 2014; Surovtsev et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: Asymmetric distributions of ParA dimers on the nucleoid drive directed movement of DNA cargos via a Brownian-ratchet mechanism.
source: These new data are consistent with a model whereby asymmetric distributions of ParA dimers on the nucleoid drive directed and persistent movement of DNA cargos (e.g. plasmids) towards increased concentrations of ParA via a Brownian-ratchet mechanism that does not require a cytoskeletal element.
evidence: This is a model supported by recent data cited in the manuscript.

claim: ParA-mediated DNA segregation requires a ParA-type ATPase that dimerizes and non-specifically binds the nucleoid in the presence of ATP.
source: ParA-mediated DNA segregation via this proposed mechanism requires only three factors: (i) a ParA-type ATPase that dimerizes and non-specifically binds the nucleoid in the presence of ATP (Leonard et al., 2005; Hester and Lutkenhaus, 2007; Castaing et al., 2008; Vecchiarelli et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ParA-mediated DNA segregation requires a partner protein ParB that site-specifically binds DNA and stimulates ParA ATPase activity.
source: (ii) a partner protein, ParB, that site-specifically binds DNA and stimulates the ATPase activity of ParA to displace it from the nucleoid (Davis et al., 1992; Bouet and Funnell, 1999; Bouet et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ParA-mediated DNA segregation requires a centromere-like site (parS) on the DNA cargo that ParB loads onto.
source: (iii) a centromere-like site on the DNA cargo (parS) that ParB loads onto (Davis and Austin, 1988; Funnell, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Multiple dimers of ParB form a large protein-DNA complex around the parS site.
source: In this model, multiple dimers of ParB form a large protein-DNA complex around the parS site, which leads to a break in ParA symmetry across the nucleoid due to the formation of local ParA depletion zones around individual ParB-bound cargos (Adachi et al., 2006; Hatano et al., 2007; Hwang et al., 2013; Vecchiarelli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: No factors analogous to ParB or parS have been identified for McdA.
source: Additionally, no factors suitable to play a role analogous to ParB or parS have been identified for McdA, preventing any direct assessment of a putative Brownian ratchet-based mechanism for carboxysomal organization.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: McdA-GFP-His significantly shifted non-specific DNA in the presence of ATP.
source: We observed that McdA-GFP-His significantly shifted non-specific DNA (nsDNA) in the presence of ATP (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: McdA-GFP-His uniformly bound DNA carpet when infused with ATP.
source: Consistent with EMSA analysis, McdA-GFP-His uniformly bound the DNA carpet when infused into the flowcell with ATP, (Figure 1B and Video 1)
evidence: This is supported by TIRFM data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1.

claim: McdA-GFP-His showed no appreciable DNA binding when ADP, ATP-γ-S were added, or when nucleotides were omitted.
source: but showed no appreciable DNA binding when ADP or ATP-γ-S were added, or when nucleotides were omitted (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by TIRFM data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No McdA filaments were observed forming under any tested conditions.
source: No McdA filaments were observed forming under any of these conditions (Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by TIRFM observations in Video 1.

claim: Native C-terminally tagged McdA (McdA-mNG) did not show dynamic oscillations.
source: Interestingly, our native C-terminally tagged reporter (McdA-mNG) did not show dynamic oscillations and instead formed a uniform distribution of signal along the longitudinal axis (≥99% of cells; n = 950 cells) (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Table 1.).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: mNG-McdA oscillations have a periodicity of 15.3 min per 3.3 µm.
source: Alternatively, an N-terminally tagged reporter (mNG-McdA) displayed robust oscillations (≥99% of cells; n = 442 cells) (periodicity of 15.3 min per 3.3 µm,~5–6 x faster than previously reported using McdA-GFP [Savage et al., 2010])
evidence: This is a measurement from microscopy data.

claim: mNG-McdA oscillations are approximately 5-6 times faster than previously reported using McdA-GFP.
source: (periodicity of 15.3 min per 3.3 µm,~5–6 x faster than previously reported using McdA-GFP [Savage et al., 2010])
evidence: This is a comparison to previously published data.

claim: Cells bearing the mNG-McdA construct maintained carboxysome positioning along the longitudinal axis.
source: Cells bearing the mNG-McdA construct maintained carboxysome positioning along the longitudinal axis (≥99% of cells; n = 374 cells) (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and Video 3)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1F and Video 3.

claim: The topology of mNG-McdA signal closely resembled that of the DAPI-stained nucleoid.
source: We found that the topology of the mNG-McdA signal closely resembled that of the DAPI-stained nucleoid (Figure 1H)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: His-MBP-McdA shifted nsDNA in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: Consistent with our McdA-GFP-His EMSA, His-MBP-McdA shifted nsDNA in an ATP-dependent manner (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: ATP-bound McdA binds DNA.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that ATP-bound N- or C-terminally tagged McdA binds DNA and McdA-GFP-His does not display indications of polymer formation at the resolution limits of our microscope.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: McdA-GFP-His does not display indications of polymer formation at the resolution limits of the microscope.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that ATP-bound N- or C-terminally tagged McdA binds DNA and McdA-GFP-His does not display indications of polymer formation at the resolution limits of our microscope.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from TIRFM observations.

claim: Deletion of pANL parB did not disrupt oscillation of mNG-McdA.
source: However, deletion of pANL parB did not disrupt oscillation of mNG-McdA (≥99% of cells; n = 554 cells) (Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Deletion of Synpcc7942_1835 had no observable effect on mNG-McdA oscillation.
source: While deletion of Synpcc7942_1835 had no observable effect on mNG-McdA oscillation (≥99% of cells; n = 834 cells) (Figure 2C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Deletion of Synpcc7942_1834 resulted in complete loss of mNG-McdA dynamics.
source: deletion of Synpcc7942_1834 resulted in complete loss of mNG-McdA dynamics (≥99% of cells; n = 373 cells). In the ΔSynpcc7942_1834 background, mNG-McdA concentrated in the center of the cell in the vicinity of the nucleoid, but without any consistent asymmetrical patterning (Figure 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: McdB lacks homology to any known ParB family member.
source: Bioinformatic analysis of the McdB protein by BlastP (protein-protein blast) revealed that McdB lacked homology to any known ParB family member, nor any identifiable conserved regions with known ParB proteins.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: McdB possesses a secondary structure consisting mainly of alpha-helices.
source: We therefore used the jPred4 platform (Drozdetskiy et al., 2015) to analyze this 17 kDa protein, which predicted that McdB possesses a secondary structure consisting mainly of alpha-helices, a highly charged N-terminal a1-helix, and a coiled-coil C-terminal a8-helix (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction using jPred4.

claim: McdA and McdB can self-associate in bacterial two-hybrid analysis.
source: McdA and McdB were able to self-associate in the B2H analysis.
evidence: This is supported by bacterial two-hybrid data.

claim: N-terminally tagged McdA interacts with N-terminally tagged McdB.
source: We also observed a reciprocal interaction between N-terminally tagged McdA and N-terminally tagged McdB (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial two-hybrid data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: S. elongatus McdA lacks the signature amino terminal lysine residue in the Walker-A motif.
source: Interestingly, S. elongatus McdA lacks the signature amino terminal lysine residue (Figure 2G)
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: His-MBP-McdA displayed strong ATPase activity alone, significantly higher (>200 fold) than that of traditional ParA family ATPases SopA and ParA.
source: His-MBP-McdA displayed strong ATPase activity alone, significantly higher (>200 fold) than that of traditional ParA family ATPases SopA of F plasmid and ParA of P1 plasmid (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The specific ATPase activity of His-MBP-McdA declined at higher protein concentrations.
source: Relative to the constant specific activity of F SopA-His and P1 ParA with increasing protein concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), the specific ATPase activity of His-MBP-McdA declined at higher protein concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity assay data.

claim: McdB-His stimulated His-MBP-McdA ATPase activity synergistically with nsDNA.
source: When both nsDNA and McdB-His were added simultaneously, the ATPase activity of His-MBP-McdA was further stimulated (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity assay data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Increasing concentrations of McdB-His resolved the gel shift provided by His-MBP-McdA and ATP.
source: Conversely, when the experiment was conducted with a constant concentration of His-MBP-McdA (2.5 µM), the shift in DNA mobility was reversed by addition of increasing amounts of McdB-His (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: McdB-His alone did not exhibit any DNA binding activity.
source: McdB-His alone did not exhibit any DNA binding activity in our gel shift assay (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: C-terminal fusions of McdB displayed a diffuse localization with random punctate-like patterns.
source: C-terminal fusions of McdB displayed a diffuse localization with random punctate-like patterns (≥99% of cells; n = 371 cells) (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: N-terminal mNG-McdB was observed as multiple discrete fluorescent foci near the central longitudinal axis of the cell.
source: In contrast, N-terminal mNG-McdB was observed as multiple discrete fluorescent foci near the central longitudinal axis of the cell (≥99% of cells; n = 699 cells), a result that strongly resembles the localization pattern of native carboxysomes (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: mNG-McdB and RbcS-mTQ signals strongly colocalized.
source: Both the mNG-McdB and RbcS-mTQ signals strongly colocalized (≥99% of cells; Pearson's Correlation Coefficient [PCC]=0.92; n = 316 cells) as fluorescent foci near the long central axis of the cell (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3C with quantitative PCC analysis.

claim: N-terminally tagged McdB interacts with shell proteins CcmK2, CcmK3, CcmK4, CcmL, and CcmO, but not CcmP.
source: Using N- or C-terminally tagged McdA or McdB as bait, the assay suggested only N-terminally tagged McdB interacts with the shell proteins CcmK2, CcmK3, CcmK4, CcmL, and CcmO, but not CcmP (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial two-hybrid data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: McdA did not show direct interaction with carboxysome shell proteins.
source: In contrast, we did not find evidence for direct interaction between McdA and carboxysome shell proteins (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial two-hybrid data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: mNG-McdB signal was diffuse in the absence of carboxysomes (ΔccmK2LMNO background).
source: We therefore examined the localization of mNG-McdB in a ΔccmK2LMNO background and found that mNG-McdB signal was diffuse (≥99% of cells; n = 389 cells) in the absence of carboxysomes (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: In the absence of carboxysomes, mNG-McdA did not oscillate and formed a homogenous distribution along the nucleoid.
source: Interestingly, in the absence of carboxysomes, mNG-McdA did not oscillate and formed a homogenous distribution along the nucleoid similar to that of our mNG-McdA∆mcdB strain (≥99% of cells; n = 227 cells) (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: mNG-McdA signal did not oscillate in ∆mcdB lines.
source: As before, mNG-McdA distributed along the nucleoid and did not oscillate in ∆mcdB lines (≥99% of cells; n = 373 cells) (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Carboxysomes in ∆mcdB lines were observed as large irregularly shaped polar fluorescent foci with smaller randomly distributed signals.
source: and carboxysomes were observed as large irregularly shaped polar fluorescent foci with smaller randomly distributed signals within the cell (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In ∆mcdA lines, mTQ-McdB still localized to carboxysomes.
source: In ∆mcdA lines, mTQ-McdB still localized to carboxysomes, indicating McdA is not required for the association (≥99% of cells; PCC = 0.85; 416 cells).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data with quantitative PCC analysis.

claim: Carboxysomes in ∆mcdA lines frequently clustered in close proximity rather than distributing throughout the cell.
source: Carboxysomes also formed large fluorescent foci in ∆mcdA lines and, where multiple foci could be resolved, they frequently clustered in close proximity rather than distributing throughout the cell (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the absence of both mcdA and mcdB, carboxysomes appeared as irregular foci of varying sizes randomly distributed through the cell.
source: In the absence of both mcdA and mcdB, carboxysomes appeared as irregular foci of varying sizes randomly distributed through the cell (≥99% of cells; n = 399 cells) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Upon overexpression of mNG-McdA, loss of McdA oscillation and formation of large irregularly-shaped RbcS-mO fluorescent foci were observed.
source: Upon the overexpression of mNG-McdA, we observed loss of McdA oscillation and the formation of large irregularly-shaped RbcS-mO fluorescent foci reminiscent of ∆mcdA, ∆mcdB and ∆mcdAB lines (≥99% of cells; n = 340 cells) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Upon overexpression of mTQ-McdB, mTQ-McdB signal colocalized at irregularly-shaped RbcS-mO fluorescent foci.
source: Upon overexpression of mTQ-McdB, we observed mTQ-McdB signal colocalized at irregularly-shaped RbcS-mO fluorescent foci as well as diffuse within the cell (≥99% of cells; PCC = 0.80; n = 345 cells) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Larger RbcS-mO bar-shaped structures were occasionally observed upon McdB overexpression.
source: Moreover, we occasionally observed (<10% of cells) much larger RbcS-mO bar-shaped structures within the cell (Figure 4E; yellow arrow)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Carboxysomes move towards the highest local concentration of McdA on the nucleoid.
source: In time-lapse experiments of mNG-McdA and RbcS-mTQ strains, we frequently observed that carboxysomes move towards the highest local concentration of McdA on the nucleoid; this was especially apparent as the wavefront of the oscillating McdA pool approaches carboxysomes (Videos 3–5).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Videos 3-5.

claim: With one carboxysome, mNG-McdA signal remained evenly distributed except for a depletion zone in the vicinity of the carboxysome.
source: In the presence of 1 carboxysome, mNG-McdA signal remained evenly distributed except for a depletion zone that correlated with the nucleoid region in the vicinity of the carboxysome (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: With two carboxysomes, mNG-McdA signal distributed along the nucleoid but was depleted in areas correlating to carboxysomes.
source: Likewise, with two carboxysomes, mNG-McdA signal again distributed along the nucleoid but was depleted in areas correlating to carboxysomes (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: mNG-McdA signal was highly reduced in areas of RbcS-mTQ signal (PCC = 0.20).
source: In either case, mNG-McdA signal was highly reduced in areas of RbcS-mTQ signal (≥99% of cells; PCC = 0.20; n = 391 cells)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy analysis with PCC measurement.

claim: One carboxysome could be clearly observed to move in the direction of the higher McdA concentration.
source: In instances where cells contained two, closely spaced carboxysomes, one carboxysome could be clearly observed to move in the direction of the higher McdA concentration (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: When sufficient distance was reached between two carboxysomes, mNG-McdA was re-recruited to the depleted nucleoid region between them.
source: When a sufficient distance was reached between the two carboxysomes, mNG-McdA was re-recruited to the depleted nucleoid region between the two carboxysomes (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Following induction with IPTG, multiple carboxysomes formed throughout cells and mNG-McdA oscillations emerged.
source: Following induction with IPTG, multiple carboxysomes formed throughout cells and mNG-McdA oscillations emerged (≥99% of cells; n = 439 cells; Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Carboxysomes displayed a hexagonal packing phenomenon where the linear arrangement along the longitudinal axis looked kinked or displayed a zig-zag pattern.
source: In addition to linear distributions, we also routinely observed carboxysomes that were equidistant to each other, but no longer linearly arranged (Figure 7A). Instead, carboxysomes displayed a hexagonal packing phenomenon where the linear arrangement along the longitudinal axis looked kinked or displayed a zig-zag pattern.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Hexagonal packing was typically correlated with cells that had a high number of carboxysomes relative to the cell's length.
source: Hexagonal packing was typically correlated with cells that had a high number of carboxysomes relative to the cell's length.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data.

claim: Both linear and hexagonal carboxysome packing were observed in hyperelongated cells.
source: In cells elongated by this method, we observed both linear and hexagonal carboxysome packing (Figure 7B)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Carboxysomes in hyperelongated cells always co-localized with a nucleoid cluster.
source: Carboxysomes in hyperelongated cells always co-localized with a nucleoid cluster, as visualized by DAPI staining (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: With the Brownian-ratchet model, five or less carboxysomes will linearly distribute on a rectangular surface representative of S. elongatus' nucleoid.
source: With the Brownian-ratchet model, five or less carboxysomes will linearly distribute on a rectangular surface representative of S. elongatus' nucleoid (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling shown in Figure 7C.

claim: S. elongatus McdA had 22.5% pairwise sequence identity to the G. kilaueensis JS1 McdA-like protein.
source: BlastP determined that S. elongatus McdA had 22.5% pairwise sequence identity to the G. kilaueensis JS1 McdA-like protein, while S. elongatus McdB had only 18.4% pairwise identity to the McdB-like protein (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic sequence analysis.

claim: S. elongatus McdB had 18.4% pairwise identity to the G. kilaueensis JS1 McdB-like protein.
source: BlastP determined that S. elongatus McdA had 22.5% pairwise sequence identity to the G. kilaueensis JS1 McdA-like protein, while S. elongatus McdB had only 18.4% pairwise identity to the McdB-like protein (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic sequence analysis.

claim: mTQ-McdB(Gk) colocalized with S. elongatus carboxysomes (PCC = 0.79).
source: Despite the low primary sequence identity of McdB(Gk), we found that mTQ-McdB(Gk) colocalized with RbcS-mO (PCC = 0.79; n = 248), indicating that mTQ-McdB(Gk) can interact with S. elongatus carboxysomes (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8B with quantitative PCC analysis.

claim: McdA does not form a cytoskeletal structure.
source: Here we show that McdA-GFP homogeneously binds non-specifically to DNA, but exhibits no signs of filament formation (Figure 1A–C and Video 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vitro TIRFM data.

claim: McdA attaches to the nucleoid body at the center of the cell.
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that McdA does not form independently-standing filaments, but instead attaches to the nucleoid body at the center of the cell, using it as a scaffolding surface to support an oscillating wave from one end of the cell to the other.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Carboxysomes are tethered to the nucleoid through interactions with McdB.
source: We provide evidence that carboxysomes are in turn tethered to the nucleoid through interactions with McdB, that in turn can bind McdA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data showing McdB localization and interactions.

claim: McdB is a novel protein bearing no identifiable sequence similarity to any known ParB proteins.
source: McdB is an even more divergent protein, bearing no identifiable sequence similarity to any known ParB proteins; indeed, no homologous proteins have been characterized in other species.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: McdB recognizes and binds a large protein-based cargo (carboxysomes).
source: This novel protein also recognizes and binds a large protein-based cargo (carboxysomes; Figure 3C,F,H), further distinguishing it from all characterized ParB-like proteins that recognize genetic cargo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing McdB localization to carboxysomes.

claim: A pool of McdB enriched at the carboxysome is necessary to locally deplete McdA.
source: Furthermore, we observe that a pool of McdB enriched at the carboxysome is necessary to locally deplete McdA (Figures 4 and 6B–D)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 4 and 6B-D.

claim: McdB has a distinct evolutionary origin from ParB-family members.
source: The parallels between features of the McdAB system and Brownian ratchet ParAB models make it tempting to speculate that McdB has a distinct evolutionary origin from ParB-family members, but that these independent protein families convergently evolved to use nucleoid gradients of ParA-like proteins to segregate entirely different classes of macromolecular structures.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed similarities and differences between McdAB and ParAB systems.

claim: McdB-carboxysome shell interactions are mediated by structural and/or charge features common to many distinct shell proteins.
source: Taken together with the evidence that a McdB homolog from G. kilaueensis JS1 with low sequence-identity still concentrated upon S. elongatus carboxysomes (Figure 8B), the most parsimonious hypothesis is that McdB-carboxysome shell interactions are mediated by structural and/or charge features common to many distinct shell proteins.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on experimental observations and structural knowledge.

claim: McdA oscillation itself might be a byproduct of the motion of multiple carboxysomes removing McdA along the nucleoid.
source: One possibility is that McdA oscillation itself might be a byproduct of the motion of multiple carboxysomes removing McdA along the nucleoid.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed to explain the emergence of McdA oscillations.

claim: The global dynamics of McdA oscillation are dependent upon a balanced level of activities between McdA and McdB.
source: An alternative hypothesis is that the global dynamics of McdA oscillation are dependent upon a balanced level of activities between McdA and McdB.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed to explain McdA oscillation dynamics.

claim: McdA and McdB may act to directly regulate the size or shape of microcompartments as they are formed.
source: While we cannot rule out the possibility of indirect effects, it is intriguing to speculate that McdA and McdB may act to directly regulate the size or shape of microcompartments as they are formed.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on observed changes in carboxysome ultrastructure.

claim: The relative ratio between McdA and McdB activities may play a role in the differences in carboxysome sizes observed under different environmental conditions or within different species.
source: The relative ratio between McdA and McdB activities may play a role in the differences in carboxysome sizes observed under different environmental conditions or within different species.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on observed effects of McdA/McdB levels on carboxysome size.

claim: The linear arrangement of carboxysomes in rod-shaped cells is largely a byproduct of nucleoid geometry, and thus, cell morphology.
source: We suggest that the linear arrangement of carboxysomes in rod-shaped cells is largely a byproduct of nucleoid geometry, and thus, cell morphology.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from computational modeling and observations in different cell morphologies.

claim: mcdA/B-like sequences frequently fall in regions near α- and β-carboxysome operons.
source: We find that mcdA/B-like sequences frequently fall in regions near α- and β-carboxysome operons (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 8C.
